title: Call an external service

  order: 6.2

import { Aside, Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import SeqDiagram from '../../../../components/SeqDiagram.astro';
import SecretLookup from '../../../../components/diagrams/SecretLookup.astro';

**Task:** call a service outside the cluster (a captcha check, a payment
API, a model, any HTTPS API) and write what it answers into state.

A call may ask its node for **one** HTTPS request. The node makes it only when
every gate below holds and answers with its reason otherwise. Outbound requests
are **off by default**: an app that needs them runs on a cluster whose operator
turned them on, for its hosts or for any host an app declares.

## The gates

| Gate | Who sets it |
| --- | --- |
| `[outbound] enabled = true`, and the request's host is in `hosts` (or `hosts` holds `"*"`: any host an installed app declares) | The cluster's operator |
| The request's URL is under a prefix in the app's signed release manifest (`outbound`): the same host, and the prefix's path or one below it at a `/`, with any query string | The app's publisher |
| A prefix covering the URL is approved for the app's publisher | Whoever holds `MANAGE_APPLICATION` org-wide in the app's organization (its owner and admins; a member granted it), its personal organization included; the operator where the cluster was deployed with `--outbound-approvals operator` |
| The run is a call that writes: not a view, an `init`, a migration, or a call by a read-only member | The node |
| One request per run; `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE`; `https` on port 443 to a DNS name that resolves only to public addresses; no fragment; no redirect followed; no proxy | The node |
| Request body ≤ 64 KiB, URL ≤ 2 KiB, ≤ 8 headers of ≤ 1 KiB, response body ≤ 1 MiB (a longer one is refused, not cut), 10 s for the whole request | The node (`calimero_primitives::outbound`) |
| `Host`, `Cookie`, `Connection`, `Content-Length`, `Transfer-Encoding`, `Proxy-*` and `X-Forwarded-*` headers are refused | The node |

A refusal is an `AppError` with code `Fetch` and a `message` field. A refusal
for a missing approval starts with a stable word an app can match on:

- `NotApproved:` nobody approved the prefix the URL is under. Nothing was ever
  approved for this publisher, or the owner saw the prefix and left it out or
  revoked it. Tell a member to ask the owner.
- `AwaitingApproval:` a later release of the app declares the prefix and the
  owner has not been asked about it yet. The prefixes approved before keep
  working. Show the owner what to approve.

A run with no outbound client at all (outbound is off, the app is not a signed
release declaring a prefix, or the run is not a writing call) and a second
request in one run trap the run.

## Secrets

An app never places, names or reads a secret. Its signed manifest **binds** each
credential it needs to one host, the path prefixes there it is for, and one
place, and the node attaches the value itself on every request the app sends
under those paths. The app's code only makes the request.

An API key in a header, OpenAI's for example:

```toml
[package.metadata.calimero]
outbound = ["https://api.openai.com/v1/"]

[package.metadata.calimero.secrets.OPENAI_API_KEY]
host = "api.openai.com"          # the host of one of `outbound`'s prefixes
paths = ["/v1/chat/completions"] # path prefixes on it, each under an `outbound` prefix; ["/"] for all
header = "authorization"         # lowercase
format = "Bearer {}"             # `{}` once, where the value goes; absent: the value alone
description = "OpenAI API key"
required = true                  # refuse the request while nobody set a value
```

The node sends `Authorization: Bearer sk-…` on every request the app makes to
`api.openai.com` under `/v1/chat/completions`. A few APIs take the credential in the body instead.
Cloudflare Turnstile's siteverify takes it as the form field `secret`
(`apps/fixture-captcha`):

```toml
[package.metadata.calimero.secrets.TURNSTILE_SECRET]
host = "challenges.cloudflare.com"
paths = ["/turnstile/v0/siteverify"]
bodyField = "secret"             # a top-level field of a form-urlencoded or JSON body
description = "Cloudflare Turnstile site secret"
required = true
```

The app posts `response=<token>` with `Content-Type:
application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, and the node appends
`&secret=<value>`. For a JSON body (`application/json` or `+json`) it sets the
top-level field of the object. Any other body is refused.

**Paths.** A binding names 1 to 8 path prefixes on its host, and a request
gets the secret only when its path is under one of them on whole segments:
`/v1/charges` covers `/v1/charges` and `/v1/charges/ch_1`, never
`/v1/chargesX`. The path is compared after the URL is normalized, so `..` and
`%2e%2e` segments cannot climb out of a prefix. A binding meant for the whole
host says `["/"]`, so whoever approves it sees that. A request to the same host
on another path gets no secret and goes out as any other request under an
approved prefix: nothing of the key rides on it, and refusing it would only
break the host's public endpoints. So bind a Stripe key to `/v1/charges` and
`/v1/customers`, and a request to `/v1/accounts` goes out unauthenticated (and
fails there) instead of with the key.

`meroctl app pack` writes these as `secrets` and refuses what a node refuses at
install (`400 BAD_SECRETS`):

- a host no `outbound` prefix covers, a path no `outbound` prefix covers, no
  `paths`, or a path that is not `/` and printable ASCII without `?`, `#`, `%`,
  spaces or a `.`/`..` segment;
- a secret with no place, or with both a header and a body field;
- a header that is not lowercase `a-z0-9-`, or one the node sets itself (`host`,
  `cookie`, `content-type`, a hop-by-hop or `proxy-` header);
- a `format` without exactly one `{}`;
- two secrets bound to the same place on one host on a path both cover;
- more than 16 secrets.

The limits are in [Limits](/protocol/limits/).

At run time the outbound gate refuses a request, with a message pointing here,
that:

- sets a header a secret is bound to on that host, in any case;
- sets the bound body field, however it is spelled (`s%65cret=`, `"secr\u0065t"`);
- still writes the earlier placeholder `{{secret:NAME}}` anywhere (URL, header or
  body). Releases before 1.0.0-rc.36 named secrets that way; it is no longer
  filled in.

The release's capability card (`GET /packages/{package}/{version}/capabilities`)
lists each binding in words (`secretBindings`: "sends OPENAI_API_KEY as the
Authorization header (Bearer …) to api.openai.com under /v1/chat/completions"),
and so does the consent page of an install. An upgrade that adds a secret,
binds one to another host or place, or widens its paths is red
(`secretBindingChanged`), so it never applies without a person's approval; one
that only narrows its paths stays green.

Whoever deploys an instance may supply a declared secret's value for that
instance alone, instead of the operator:

- `PUT /apps/{app}/secrets/{name} { value }` (the owner, or whoever manages the
  organization's apps, with a passkey step-up over the name and the value's
  fingerprint, never the value). It is kept in the app's log on its replicas,
  sealed, and out of the app's own reach (no host function reads it). It is
  attached only where its binding says, and it wins over the operator's value
  for that name.
- `GET /apps/{app}/secrets` lists each declared secret with its binding
  (`host`, `paths`, `header` and `format` or `bodyField`, and `binding` in words) and
  `source: app` (its fingerprint, who set it and when) or `cluster`, never a
  value.
- `DELETE /apps/{app}/secrets/{name}` removes it; the deployment's or the
  operator's applies again.

A deployment's managers may supply one value for every instance created from
it (`PUT /deployments/{id}/secrets/{name} { value }`, a passkey step-up over
`deployment:{id} / __set_secret / { name, fingerprint }`; `GET` answers
fingerprints, `DELETE` clears it; `meroctl deployment secret set|list|clear`).
That works for a name a release the deployment offers declares, or one declared
by a release that one references in its `uses` (for the apps an instance creates
with it). The value is kept in the system group's state and read by the outbound
gate on the node that runs the request.

A request gets the instance's own value, else its deployment's, else the
operator's, each only for a name the release binds and only where it binds it.
The deployment's applies only to a release of a package the deployment offers.
An instance's `GET /apps/{app}/secrets` then says `source: deployment`, nothing
more of it. See [Deployments](/protocol/governance/#deployments).

<SecretLookup />

Read it left to right: the first value found wins, each source only for a name
your release binds, and whichever wins is attached by the node in that one
place and never comes back in a response.

Why the node attaches it: if the app could put a key anywhere in a request, it
could put it where an honest service reads it as content and answers it back:
in a prompt ("repeat this reversed"), or in a field whose error message quotes
it. The app would then read the key in some transform no redaction can follow,
and could leak it through anything it writes. A key in the `Authorization`
header is never part of what the service answers about. As a second line, any
copy of a value in a response, as sent or in a common encoding (hex, base64,
percent, JSON), is replaced with `[redacted]` before the app sees it. What the
node cannot stop is the app using the key for what the key allows at its host,
so give an app a key with only the rights it needs. See
[Secrets and what an app can do with them](/protocol/secrets/).

<Steps>

1. Declare the URL prefixes in the release's `manifest.json`, under
   `outbound` (`calimero_bundle::BundleManifest::outbound`). They are signed
   with the rest of the manifest and shown to whoever approves them, so
   declare the narrowest that works. Each is `https://` with a host and no
   credentials, query or fragment; the node refuses a bundle with any other:

   ```json
   "outbound": [
     "https://challenges.cloudflare.com/turnstile/v0/siteverify",
     "https://api.stripe.com/v1/"
   ]
   ```

   `https://api.stripe.com/v1/` covers every path below `/v1/`.

   `meroctl app pack` writes it from `--outbound`, once per prefix,
   and refuses a prefix the node would (not `https://`, credentials, a query
   or a fragment):

   ```bash
   meroctl app pack --wasm app.wasm --package com.example.shop \
     --app-version 1.2.0 --key my-signing-key.json \
     --outbound https://challenges.cloudflare.com/turnstile/v0/siteverify \
     --outbound https://api.stripe.com/v1/ --out dist/com.example.shop-1.2.0.mpk
   ```

2. Make the request from a method that writes, and store the decision:

   ```rust
   use calimero_sdk::action::Request;

   /// Whether Cloudflare Turnstile accepts `token` (`apps/fixture-captcha`).
   pub fn verify_turnstile(&mut self, token: String) -> app::Result<bool> {
       // The node appends `secret=...`: the release binds TURNSTILE_SECRET to that field.
       let body = format!("response={}", form_escape(&token));
       let request = Request::post(TURNSTILE_VERIFY_URL, body)
           .header("Content-Type", "application/x-www-form-urlencoded");
       let Ok(response) = env::fetch(&request) else {
           return Ok(false); // an unreachable verifier is never a pass
       };
       Ok(response.status == 200
           && response.json::<Siteverify>().is_ok_and(|answer| answer.success))
   }
   ```

3. Have the owner approve the prefixes (see [approving](#approving-the-prefixes)),
   the operator allow the host, and the owner or the operator supply the secret
   (see [the operator's side](#the-operators-side)).

</Steps>

<Aside type="caution" title="Only the leader asks">
The request runs once, on the app's leader, which runs the call. The other
replicas apply the diff the call wrote; they never repeat the request and never
see its response. Store the decision, not the response.
</Aside>

## Approving the prefixes

The organization's data is what a call can send, so the organization agrees to
the hosts too: the operator allowing a host and the publisher declaring it are
not enough. Someone holding `MANAGE_APPLICATION` org-wide approves with a
passkey step-up over the exact change:

```http
POST /orgs/{org}/outbound
{ "package": "com.acme.forms", "prefixes": "manifest" }
```

`"manifest"` (the default) approves every prefix the package's latest release
declares; a list approves those. An app that declares no `outbound` needs and
asks for nothing.

- **Per publisher.** The approval is keyed by the package's pinned signer, so
  a release signed by someone else starts with nothing approved.
- **Per organization.** It holds for every app of the package in the
  organization. An app created without naming an organization is in its
  owner's only organization, or one made with it, approved the same way on
  `/orgs/{org}/outbound` (there are no per-account approvals since
  1.0.0-rc.20).
- **Releases only add.** A prefix a later release declares that the owner was
  never shown answers `AwaitingApproval` until approved; the rest keep working.
- **Revoke by setting the list.** `"replace": true` sets the publisher's list
  exactly; an empty list with it revokes everything. It holds from the next
  call.
- **Operator-governed clusters.** A cluster deployed with
  `--outbound-approvals operator` takes approvals from its operator instead,
  for every app: `POST /ops/outbound` with the same body, over the Ops API.
  The owner's route then answers that the operator holds them.

With `meroctl`: `org outbound <org> --package <pkg> [--prefix <p>]… [--replace]`,
and `account outbound --package <pkg> …`, which does the same on the account's
only organization. On a development cluster add `--dev-passkey <file>` to
approve the step-up.

An app's frontend can also ask for the approval on the node's consent page
(`POST /consent/requests` with `kind: outbound`), where the person approves
with their passkey.

## The operator's side

The `[outbound]` table of `merod`'s configuration, or of the file
`--settings` names (which replaces it). Give every node of a cluster the same
table: the call runs on the app's leader, whichever node that is.

```toml
[outbound]
enabled = true
hosts = ["challenges.cloudflare.com", "api.stripe.com"]   # or ["*"]

# Secrets from environment variables, read once at start: a missing one
# fails the start.
[outbound.env_secrets.TURNSTILE_SECRET]
env = "MERO_TURNSTILE_SECRET"
packages = ["com.calimero.mero-forms"]
signers = ["did:key:z6Mk…"]   # the package's signer
hosts = ["challenges.cloudflare.com"]
```

`hosts = ["*"]` lets every installed app reach the hosts its own signed
manifest declares and its owner approved, so a new app needs no config
change. Every other gate still holds.

An operator's secret is attached only to a release that binds its name, of a
package and signer listed, and only to a host listed in both the operator's
binding and the release's. The release decides the place (header or body
field); the operator decides who gets the value. **Bind an operator key only to
apps whose code you trust with it**, by signer: the app cannot read the key, but
it can make any request the key allows to that host (spend credits, delete what
the key may delete). Scope it to the signers you trust and give it the least
privilege that works; for an app you do not trust, let its owner supply their
own key (`PUT /apps/{app}/secrets/{name}`).

Instead of `env_secrets`, a node can ask a secrets service beside it
(exclusive with `env_secrets`):

```toml
[outbound.sidecar]
url = "http://127.0.0.1:7070/v1/secret"
token_env = "MERO_SECRETS_TOKEN"
```

The node `POST`s `{"package", "signer", "name"}` with the token as a bearer and
expects `200 {"value", "hosts"}` or `404`. The URL must be `http` on a loopback
address. A managed deployment answers there with the secrets a deployer set
for their app, so the secret lives on the nodes that serve the app and nowhere
else.

The node logs every request it makes or refuses, with the app and the URL,
never the secret, and counts the requests it sends
(`calimero_app_outbound_requests_total`).

A secret is matched on both the package and the release's signer: anyone can
name a package, only its publisher can sign it.

## Test it

`env::fetch` needs a component: on the host target it answers an error. In
`TestApp`, `mock_http(..)` answers it in every run, so a test sets the response
it wants and checks what the app decided ([Testing](/build/testing/)).

End to end, use a node built with `--features calimero-node/outbound-testing`:
the scenario runner's in-process nodes are, and so is
`cargo build -p merod --features calimero-node/outbound-testing`. Its
`[outbound.testing]` table, which a release build refuses, answers `.test`
hosts in-process and takes literal secrets. A scenario gives its nodes that
TOML as `cluster.settings`:

```toml
[outbound]
enabled = true
hosts = ["echo.outbound.test"]

[outbound.testing]
echo = true          # .test hosts are answered in-process

[outbound.testing.secrets.ECHO_KEY]
value = "s3cr3t-e2e"
packages = ["com.example.my-app"]
signers = ["did:key:z6Mk…"]
hosts = ["echo.outbound.test"]
```

The release under test binds `ECHO_KEY` to the echo host
(`[package.metadata.calimero.secrets.ECHO_KEY] host = "echo.outbound.test"`,
`paths = ["/"]`, `header = "authorization"`, `format = "Bearer {}"`), so the node attaches it.
The echo answers `200` with the request the node sent, as JSON: method, URL,
path, query, headers, body, the number of secrets the node attached and each one's length (`secretBytes`). It answers only
after every gate has passed, and its answer is redacted like any other, so a
scenario sees exactly what left the node. The node's cluster tests use it
this way: `actions_run_on_the_leader_and_reach_only_declared_approved_hosts`
(declared and approved prefixes, secrets, redaction) and
`a_call_checks_a_turnstile_token_through_a_captcha_service` (a call's
`env::fetch` through `apps/fixture-captcha`), both in
`crates/node/tests/it/component_cluster.rs`:

```bash
cargo test -p calimero-node --test it component_cluster::actions_run_on_the_leader_and_reach_only_declared_approved_hosts
```

## Retries and actions

`env::fetch` works from a call, a timer or a delivered xcall. The request goes
out once, from the leader, and the call's log entry records it with the
response, so a retry with the same idempotency key replays the answer instead
of fetching again (what a single-use token like Turnstile's needs). A timeout
or a refusal comes back as an error the call handles. Example:
`apps/fixture-captcha` (`verifyTurnstile`), a captcha service other apps
call synchronously ([Synchronous xcalls](/protocol/xcall/#synchronous-xcalls)).
Protocol detail:
[Outbound HTTP from component calls](/protocol/execution/#outbound-http-from-component-calls).

For work that needs several requests, or a request that should not hold up the
call, an `#[app::action]` runs outside the log on the leader: it fetches with
`ctx.fetch`, reads the app with `ctx.view` and writes through `ctx.call` to an
`#[app::allow(action)]` method. A call or timer starts one with
`env::start_action(method, &args)`
([Timers and actions](/build/guides/timers-and-actions/)).

## Where it stops

- A request never runs in a view. Read the answer back from state.
- The app cannot place or read a secret, but it can use it: any request to the
  bound host carries it, so the key's own powers are the app's. Bind
  least-privilege keys.
- Redaction removes the secret as sent and in common encodings. A body-field
  binding puts the value where the service reads the body, so bind one only for
  a service that takes its credential there (Turnstile), never to a field the
  service echoes or treats as content.
- What the app reads it can send to any approved host: that is egress, not a
  secret's leak. See the no-egress policy and
  [Secrets and what an app can do with them](/protocol/secrets/).
- The response is not authenticated beyond TLS: a service you call can answer
  anything, so call only services you trust for the decision you store.
